doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: First jazz records, Sydney conservatory and the music store job
summary: His first jazz was Turk Murphy on radio; in Sydney he failed to fit the conservatory system and learned jazz from taping records at a music store.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: So what kind of music did you listen to when you got into your teens? Did you get into jazz recordings?

No, not at all until college. The first jazz, apart from this band that came by on the truck (I think they were playing “Saints” or something), the very first jazz I heard was Turk Murphy’s band on the radio, from the University of the Pacific radio station. And shortly after that the family emigrated to Sydney and I started looking around for jazz. I was starting to collect ‘78s and I got a big job in a music store which was good. The whole idea was for me to go — we were going to settle in a city. We could build a boat anywhere — going back to the boat — we could build a boat anywhere, but we were going to go to a city where I could get into a conservatory and finish my degree. And it was a good theory, except we wrote to all of them and the only one that wrote back was the Sydney one, and they said yeah well we’ll have a look at him. So when I got there they asked me questions like, “Well what syllabus have you been studying?” And I said, “What’s a syllabus?” And they said, “Oh, well, what grade have you achieved?” “What do you mean what grade?” They asked me all these questions because the whole thing is built on the English system of grades and the syllabus means the program and, “What piece have you prepared?” and I hadn’t prepared any piece. So I didn’t fit in at all. And I left the conservatory with a kong — as we call it there — and got a job in a music store. And I got posted to the jazz department. And all of a sudden I was able to check out records every night — like two and three LP’s. This was required, that you take home records and listen to them. Yeah. It was fantastic. So I took home everything, everything in the whole section, and taped everything. You weren’t supposed to tape it, but I taped it of course, and brought it back the next day. So I had this vast collection of all these different things, and learned a lot at that time.
